In the dense, dank heart of the rainforest, Skylar's life was brutally silenced with a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston to navigate a labyrinth of lies, offered up by the two prime suspects - Albert and Mya.

Winston entered the bustling atmosphere of a large family gathering, all clatter and congratulations on a reunion well-needed. His gaze shifted to a tall woman energetically engaging with her relatives, her vibrant energy palpable amongst the crowd. That would be Mya, the adventurous cousin of the unfortunate victim, Skylar.

He noticed the polished locket adorning her neck, catching the light beautifully, but a sombre contrast to its owner's lively charm.

Exuding friendly charm, Winston approached her, "Mya, may I have a couple of moments?"

"Of course, detective. How may I help you?"

"I understand you and Skylar used to explore your adventurous side together," Winston mentioned casually, trying not to stir any emotional discomfort.

Mya's face softened, "Yes. We both shared a love for the wilderness. Just last week, she invited me on a camping trip to the rainforest. It was harmonious escapades until…” she trailed off.

“Aye, I’m sorry for your loss, Mya.”  
 
Winston noticed the emphasis on her well-toned physique - a strong and agile body, built on a rigorous exercise routine and several hiking and mountain climbing expeditions successfully completed over the years.

Later on, Winston got an opportunity to evaluate the surveillance video of the day Skylar went missing. A quiet scene it was, with only a single instance of incoming and no outgoing traffic - a four-wheel-drive carrying two adventurous souls - Skylar and Mya - into the depths of the rainforest.

Winston’s keen eyes caught the glimpse of Mya’s camping gear. It sure was well stocked - ropes, food supplies, a lead pipe, tents, boots… A lead pipe. The very same, that had turned brutal enough to end a life in the tranquil rainforest.

At Mya’s, while she was away, Winston could only find her camping gear partially scattered in disarray. The lead pipe was blatantly missing.

In a cruiser parked down the street, Winston watched Mya jog up to the deadly rainforest, maybe a run to process her grief, or maybe it was part of her regular exercise routine. Winston watched Mya stoop suddenly and pick something up. A glint of gold. Later, at the reunion, the piece was identified as Skylar’s locket around Mya’s neck. A locket that mysteriously went missing after Skylar's demise and never returned to the rightful inheritors.

Winston took a deep breath. There was so much more to untangle in the mysterious disappearance of Skylar. The case continued to thicken, deeper into the rainforest.

Casual drizzle splattered against the umbrella of Winston as he stood by the yellow cab, its windows slick with rain and partially hiding the figure inside. He knocked twice against the window before it hesitantly slid down, revealing the rough and worn face of Albert, a cab driver who had been working these city streets for longer than most would care to remember. 

"Albert," Winston began, pulling out his badge to cut off any question of his identity. "Seems like you're having a quiet night."

"Just like every other night in this forsaken city," Albert responded bitterly, his hands, the hands of a man used to hard labor, tightening around the taxi steering wheel. 

"I heard about your baseball career back in college. Must have been exciting times," Winston remarked, casually glancing at a lead pipe secured beneath the driver's seat. "Got to make sure feelings of nostalgia don't lead to some baseball practice, especially not in a city like ours."

Albert hesitated for a moment, before answering, "It's for safety. Different times…"

Winston nodded, turning towards the rainforest in the distance. Albert followed his gaze, "Crazy what happened. I was just driving her, Skylar...that is, to the rainforest. The city loved her, I've even seen people switch cabs to ride with her."

"Must have been a challenge," Winston said, subtly hinting at the power dynamics at play.

"It was more than just a challenge," Albert growled. "That woman was taking away everything I had."

"Do you know why she wanted to go to the rainforest?" Winston asked, eager to shift the focus.

"Didn't ask," Albert responded briskly. "She requested me as her driver and asked to go to the rainforest. Took a little detour, tried to show her some city charm...wouldn't say she really appreciated it though."

"Do you know if anyone else was with her there?"

"Just her," Albert answered. "As far as I knew, it was just going to be her in the rainforest. That was the last I saw."

As Winston walked away, leaving Albert with his rumbling taxi and burdensome thoughts, he pondered how volatile resentment could become if not managed properly — a flame which could engulf the careers and lives of even those most loved. The rain pattered against his umbrella, but beneath it, his mind was turning.

results.input:
In the dense, dank heart of the rainforest, Skylar's life was brutally silenced with a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston to navigate a labyrinth of lies, offered up by the two prime suspects - Albert and Mya.

Detective Winston put down Skylar's phone, there was a series of text messages that stood out to him involving an invitation to a camping trip. He sat back and scratched his chin thoughtfully as it fell into place with the CCTV footage - Skylar and Mya entering the rainforest alone.

Making a note of this, he remembered another piece of CCTV footage from two days back, showing Mya packing for what seems to be a camping trip. The footage included one notable item within her gear – a lead pipe, distinct because Mya seemed to pay particular attention to it.

He decided to pay a visit to Mya. She was found at her regular gym, her movements were fluid and strong as she exercised, her biceps straining under the weight. She was in a very good shape, her fitness wasn't in question, that was sure. As she rested between sets, Winston approached her.

“Excuse my interruption," Winston began, "I’ve read that you’ve completed quite a few hiking and mountain climbing expeditions?”

A look of surprise flashed on her face, She nodded, panting a bit. “Yes, I’ve been fortunate enough to get around…” she replied.

“You met up with Skylar for a camping trip recently?” Winston probed, her eyes flickered away, a troubled expression crossing her face. “Yes, Skylar invited me."

"I understand there’s been tension in the family recently," Winston strayed towards less comfortable territories. "Skylar had revealed something personal about you to your family, is that right?"

"The accusation about a family heirloom…" Mya tensed, glancing sharply at Winston,"That was absolutely baseless. Skylar had no reason to accuse me.” She visibly wilted, there was an anger in her voice, fueled by embarrassment. “It’s been a dark chapter in my life.”

Winston nodded, understanding. He had been briefed about Skylar revealing Mya's secret and how the family had started ostracizing her due to the false accusation.

As Mya picked up her gym bag to leave, Winston noticed her camping gear in the open compartment. The video registered in his mind. The roll of duct tape, an aluminum water bottle, a headlamp but the lead pipe was missing. The same lead pipe that was seen on the CCTV footage when she was packing. It was a small detail but something that stuck with Winston.

Outside the gym, as Winston leaned against his car, one fact bore heavily on his mind - no other cars had been recorded entering or leaving the rainforest by any of the surveillance teams on the day Skylar had been killed. This little nugget of fact had been disturbing him the entire day.

Winston's face hardened while he made the drive back to his office. His mind was whirling; he needed to look at the bigger picture. He was only making sense of each piece that he was uncovering. Whatever was happening was complex, and he had a lot of facts to untangle.

Winston strolled past the line of cabs parked near the city center. He had a destination in mind - the beaten grey vehicle at the end. The driver, Albert, was in the middle of a losing battle with his customer inflow. Not that the local populace didn't patronize taxis. In fact, Skylar was the sweetheart of the city, everyone in town loved her and seemed to prefer her company rather than Albert’s. 

“Albert, have some free time for a chat?” Winston asked as he leaned into the cab’s open window. 

Albert’s gaze didn’t leave the rear-view mirror, covered with a pile of sunglasses. “Not like I have a lot of customers waiting, detective,” he grumbled.

"Skylar seemed to be collecting quite a few of your regulars. You seemed to think she was taking away your livelihood. Did you know her well?" Winston inquired, ignoring Albert's bitter tone. 

Albert's eyebrows furrowed as he fixated on the cab’s ornament-studded dash. "We met a few times. I was her cab driver for the day. Imagine the luck.”

“Skylar requested you to drive her to the rainforest that day, didn’t she?”

Albert gave a quick nod, the beginnings of sweat forming on his forehead. "Yes, and I took a detour. Figured it would save time.” 

Winston glanced at the windshield, spotting an almost perpetual darkness, and turned back towards Albert. "You always drive at night, don't you?"

"Yeah, and?" Albert's defensive demeanor wasn’t hard to miss. 

"No reason," Winston mused, shifting to open up his field of vision. “I find it interesting,” he moved on, "because you have a large collection of shades. You know, considering your night job and all…" 

Albert laughed, a hollow sound echoing in the cab. "I don't even know what you mean by light sensitivity, detective.”

With a nod, Winston changed topics, "Did you notice anything strange about Skylar that day? Anything about her demeanor?"

Albert scratched his cheek nervously, avoiding Winston's gaze. "She seemed pretty normal to me."

"Have any issues making eye contact, for example?" Winston asked, noticing that he himself hadn’t gotten much eye contact during the discussion. 

Albert's laugh returned. It was hollow, yet somewhat nervous. “N-never been a fan, detective. Just a thing.”

"Alright, Albert. Thanks for your time." Winston straightened up, taking one last look at Albert and the cab before turning away. As far as anyone knew, nobody else was in the rainforest that day - it was just Albert, Skylar, and a host of unanswered questions. Winston had quite a lot to ponder over.

### Key Clues Pointing to Mya:
1. **Motive**: Mya had a strong personal grudge against Skylar. Skylar falsely accused Mya of stealing a family heirloom, leading to Mya being ostracized by her family. Mya expressed anger and embarrassment about this during her interview with Detective Winston, indicating a powerful emotional motive for violence.

3. **Murder Weapon Connection**: 
   - Two days before the murder, CCTV footage captured Mya packing for a camping trip, including a lead pipe. The footage highlighted her paying "particular attention" to it, suggesting its significance.
   - During Winston's visit to Mya at the gym, her camping gear (in her gym bag) contained items like duct tape, a water bottle, and a headlamp—but the lead pipe was conspicuously missing. This aligns with the murder weapon (a lead pipe) used to kill Skylar.

4. **Physical Capability**: Mya was observed at the gym demonstrating significant strength and fitness, confirming she was physically capable of wielding a lead pipe to commit the murder.

### Clues Regarding Albert:
- Albert drove Skylar to the rainforest that day and admitted to taking a detour (which could imply an attempt to avoid surveillance). However:
  - There is no direct evidence linking Albert to the murder weapon. He had no known access to a lead pipe, and no such item was mentioned in his cab or possessions.
  - His motive (Skylar stealing his customers) is weaker and more business-oriented compared to Mya's deeply personal vendetta.
  - Albert's suspicious behavior (avoiding eye contact, nervousness, and owning sunglasses despite driving at night) suggests guilt or concealment, but it is circumstantial and does not override the physical evidence against Mya.
  - Crucially, CCTV footage did not show Albert entering the rainforest with Skylar—only Skylar and Mya were seen entering together. While Albert drove Skylar, the surveillance confirmed no other cars entered or left, and he likely departed after dropping her off. The story's closing line ("it was just Albert, Skylar...") reflects Winston's initial uncertainty, but the evidence solidly places Mya at the scene with the victim.

### Conclusion:
The combination of Mya's motive, her confirmed presence with Skylar at the crime scene, and the direct link to the murder weapon (the lead pipe in her possession before the crime and missing afterward) overwhelmingly implicates her. Albert's involvement is limited to driving Skylar, with no substantive evidence tying him to the murder itself.

ANSWER: [Mya]

“Hey, Jim! your presence is needed!" announced Winston, drawing the attention of a towering, muscular figure.

“Wow, Winston, you seem all business today," replied Jim, affably, turning to face his visitor.

“You weren’t working today?” queried Winston, scrutinizing Jim's reaction. Giving a carefree shrug, Jim responded, "Yes, occasionally we get the day off, like today."

Jim's actions had a disciplined, well-practiced grace, something Winston noted was consistent with someone undergoing martial arts training. When Winston asked about his training, Jim confirmed it with a simple nod.

“So, what about the money you owed Philip?” Winston asked, causing a silence to fall over them, broken only by the sounds of crashing waves. The burden of the enormous debt to Philip weighed heavily on Jim, evidenced by his discomfort.

“Philip... He came across some... documents,” Jim confessed, his gaze focused elsewhere, “He planned to use them against me. Though, it's irrelevant now."

Soon, Winston found himself alone, watching as Jim left. After a moment’s contemplation, he figured his next action would be to visit the desert where Philip’s body was found.

Winston was walking towards the park with his hands in his pockets, dust from the trail whirling up around him as he went. His furrowed brows gave way to the seriousness he was to face discussing Philip's murder with his grandfather, Woodrow.

Woodrow was a frail looking old man. However, his frailty was physically deceptive. He was still as spry as a young deer when it came to his martial arts routine, he had been doing it every single day, religiously, after he had retired from forty long years of teaching martial arts. He was even sweating from his usual morning exercises when he walked up for their meeting.

"Winston, am I right?" Woodrow asked, nervously shifting his feet and clearing his throat constantly. To an observing party, it might almost look like nervous ticks. 

Winston nodded, not missing the unusual behavior, before he cleared his throat and asked, "You've lived in this small town all your life, Woodrow?" which the elderly man confirmed, stating that he had strong roots within his family and loved everyone fiercely. 

He held on to a coffee cup, which steamed slightly in the morning chill. He had been discussing the local park regulations with the passing-by officials while sipping slowly from the cup.

Interrupting their conversation was an unexpected arrival from a police officer, which resulted in Woodrow spilling his coffee on the cold concrete in surprise.

Inside, Winston couldn't help but get drawn towards the shelves, which displayed an array of martial arts-related memorabilia, many of which were used by Woodrow himself during his teaching years. His eyes fell on a pair of nunchaku kept securely within a glass case.

"Treasures from better times," Woodrow murmured looking at his collection.

The conversation soon shifted towards Philip. Philip, the man who had shown no remorse publicly humiliating Woodrow. Philip was a tough bone to crack, his abusive nature had managed to alienate not only Woodrow, but almost every member of their family.

"Philip was a tough man to deal with. But family is family, you know," said Woodrow before he excused himself to wash the coffee stain off his shirt. 

Winston was left staring at the array of martial arts memorabilia.

In the heart of a bustling fitness center, Heidi's life was abruptly silenced by a shotgun's blast; now it's up to the astute Detective Winston to round up suspects Grace and Chester and unravel the threads of this complex murder mystery.

Winston studied Grace's appearance as she labored over the dismantling of her shotgun, a routine she performed with a kind of measured grace that only came with practice.

"I take it hunting is a regular hobby of yours, Grace?" he asked. She straightened her back and brushed a lock of hair from her eyes, her hands still loosely holding the dismantled firearm. She nodded.

"It's tradition. Heidi and I would always go out into the wilderness, me with my nine-two shotgun, her with her ridiculous tin of marshmallows. I remember she'd always be the one who'd leave, while I'd stay at the fire, peering into the forest, not returning to the tent." Grace chuckled, but her smile didn't reach her eyes. "Even when we were out here, pushing fitness, she was looking out for safety."

"And you had a mutual workout routine both of you followed?" Winston questioned.

"Yes, every day like clockwork." She sighed. "But I convinced Heidi to change it. I argued it was safer, better for her. That night she was murdered, she implemented the change."

Winston looked at her, his sharp eyes noticing the glimmers of distress in hers. "Could that change have caused her to meet her killer?"

"She started seeing someone. I thought it was best if we changed the time, to throw off this new person. But she didn't listen..." Her voice held a slight edge, possessive almost.

As she related the details about her trips with Heidi, Winston noticed her rain-soaked hiking boots, mud-streaked pants, and her tired eyes.

"Looks like you've been out there yourself today?" he gestured at her appearance.

"Busy day," Grace responded curtly, her gaze never leaving the shotgun she was now starting to reassemble. "I usually got up the earliest. Not much point in sleeping when there's hunting to be done. The guys in the camp aren't morning people anyway."

"I see," Winston muttered, "You two, you worked out together frequently, didn't you?" 

"Heidi's the one who introduced me to working out at the fitness center. We would even do so late at night, just us, a lot of sweat and a hell of a lot of heavy lifting." She smiled at the thought, her eyes glossing over with a mixture of remembrance and grief. 

Winston nodded, scribbled down a few lines in his notepad and thanked her for her time. There was still so much to understand, so much to link together.

Sunlight filtered in through the windows of the fitness center, casting long shadows on the equipment and machines scattered around the vast room. In the corner of the spacious gym, Chester was spotted, tending to some weights when detective Winston walked in.

Chester, slight in stature, belied his physical prowess as a jockey. His wiry exterior seemed incongruent with the voracious power emanated by his presence. "Hello Chester," Winston began, his gruff voice noticeably contrasting with the calmness of the gym.

"Detective Winston, isn't it?" Chester replied with ease, his demeanor not showing a single shred of surprise or fear. Just two weeks ago, Chester had started his new gig at the fitness center, partly to make some extra bucks and partly to maintain his fitness routine. It wasn't surprising to Winston that Chester would frequently show up right when Heidi, an active member of the gym, was last seen alive.

Just when he had started to become regular at the gym, murmurs among Chester's gang had grown louder. They've started questioning his loyalties, not convinced that his regular visits to the gym were purely for maintaining his fitness.  

Their subtle talk was interrupted by the loud reverberations of gunshots in the distant background. Chester, an avid hunter, often flexed his shooting skills at the range nearby after winding up work at the gym.

"You like to shoot, huh?" Winston casually pointed towards the direction of the gun shot sounds. "Yeah. Helps take the edge off," Chester replied, a faint smile appeasing his otherwise-hardened face.

The conversation gradually led them to Heidi, a brave woman who had recently made criticisms about Chester's gang at a local town meeting. Their illegal activities were an open secret in town, countered only by the fear they instilled in those who dared to oppose. Heidi was the latest in the list, her fate tying in with an unfortunate coincidence: Chester's gang members are known to carry shotguns, the same kind that ended her life. 

Detective Winston and Chester finally diverged to their respective routines. The detective's mind was buzzing with theories, but his face was an ocean of calm. He had gathered the facts. The story had to be spun. His job could not be influenced by hasty conclusions... not when the facts all led to one presumable as intimidating as Chester.

In the eerie silence of the swamp, Jess was brutally murdered with a sai, leaving Detective Winston sorting through a mire of secrets and lies involving two prime suspects - Leona and Freya.

Winston looked out at the swamp that had claimed Jess's life. Following the cordoned path, the flash of evidence markers catching his eyes, he ran his fingers around the sai in his hand. It was of a unique make, identical to the style used in Freya's martial arts training and not commonly found. There were not many who could handle such a unique weapon, fewer still who owned them.

The path led him to Freya's home later that day. He was introduced into a crisp and clean living room, save for an empty slot in a display case filled with a fascinating collection of sais. He pondered silently, looking at the missing gap, like a puzzle awaiting to be solved, surely it must have been an important sai to her.

Off the bat, Freya seemed uncomfortable as she started nervously, "It's good to see you detective, I’m sure you've heard from my friends, they stopped by and I expressed to them my concerns about Jess threating to disclose my secrets. They comforted me, assuring me they would speak to her.”

Seeing that Freya seemed distressed, Winston decided to breach the topic divertedly, “Freya, I notice one is missing. Care to tell about it?”

With a hesitant nod, Freya spoke, “It recently went missing. The one missing held a sentimental value to me, Detective.”

"Picked up any replacements?" He asked. “Any practicing recently?”

"Well, I was at my dojo last week for training," Freya offered.

An interesting tidbit given the recent events. He was drawn by a peculiar object on a side table. A phone, separate from the one Freya had nervously returned to her pocket.

“This your personal phone, Freya?” Winston asked.

Freya’s cheeks reddened, and she quickly replied, “That's my private phone, detective. I find it easier to keep my personal lines separated from the world.” The device was quickly turned off, secure under her watchful gaze.

Throughout the conversation, she seemed uncomfortable whenever he moved too close to anything personal, quickly steering to another topic. Noted, Winston thought, but he was yet to bring up anything about Jess.

“Freya, let me cut to the chase. Jess was found to have written a letter to the local paper about exposing someone's dark secrets. We found a large payment from you to a private investigator. Want to tell me something?"

She seemed aghast. "Detective, Jess had been saying for a while that she had something on me that could ruin me. But we all have our secrets, don’t we? I hired someone to figure out what she had, it was all in my defense!”

Winston took a moment to consider her words. She was a charming woman, but he was trained to look past faces. "It's good to be honest, Freya," he added quietly, placing the sai back in the evidence bag and heading for the door. 

Once back in his car, he noted how stalwartly Freya switched off her private phone when he was around, an action that made him ponder as he started his vehicle to return to base.

Winston had never been a huge fan of pop music, he preferred jazz. Nevertheless, he found himself standing next to a stage that had, the previous night, been vibrating with the sound waves of Leona's music. Leona, a young singer with a dazzling voice that had jetted her to national stardom. Now, just twenty-four hours after her astonishing concert, she was being questioned by Winston, a detective, about the horrific discovery that morning of Jess' lifeless body beside the neighboring swamp.

He found Leona backstage, looking distraught.

"Your concert last night," Winston spoke patiently. "The venue was right next to the swamp, am I correct?”

Leona, with her tear-stained mascara, nodded. "Yes, detective. It was."

"And you had Jess present? Jess with the VIP pass?"

"Yes," Leona replied, her usually confident voice reduced to a mere whisper. "She even met my sister after the show."

"Interesting," Winston muttered, trying to keep his tone neutral. "Because I had a report that she was seen arguing with your sister. She seemed rather threatened."

Leona's face was a mask of sadness as she recalled the event. "My sister? Threatened? I...I saw it happen, she looked scared during their confrontation. Later, Jess also sent a threatening message to my sister after that confrontation. It really upset her and she's been in a distressed state since then."

Noticing the grim determination on Leona's face as her thoughts drifted to her sister, Winston probed further. "I heard you're protective of her," he added, watching Leona's reaction.

Visibly shaken, Leona admitted, "I always have been." She dabbed at her eyes with a tissue. "We only have each other. That's why I didn't object when she wanted to come to my martial arts classes."

"Ah, your martial arts classes," Winston interjected. "I have on my record here that you've been seen attending those regularly over the past months."

Leona looked surprised. "Yes, detective. I needed a way to vent out my stress, and I found martial arts comforting."

"Martial arts, hmm?" Winston mused aloud. "Your instructor even mentioned that you've been progressing quite well and he admires your skill with certain weapons. Have you ever handled a sai?"

Fear was written clear on Leona's face as she quietly nodded, understanding where this conversation might be leading to. "Yes, I have. I just purchased a set and have been training with them. They stay in the dojo, though. I swear.”

Little did Leona know, but her confession perfectly fit the narrative Winston was trying to weave. He gave nothing away with his stoic expression.

"I heard," he continued slowly, "that after the concert, Jess was seen headed towards the swamp."

She nodded her head, "Yeah, people sometimes take that route to avoid the traffic..."

The conversation ended, and Winston didn’t probe further. As far as Detective Winston was concerned, he had all the information he needed. He had many clues to ponder over and a murder investigation to lead. The image of the sai next to Jess's body in the swamp was quick to return as he went back to his car.

The muggy air of the swamp, with its accompanying sounds of buzzing insects and distant croaks of frogs, was a strange backdrop to a brutal crime. Winston's face took on a grim expression as he squinted his eyes against the setting sun, trying to piece together the final gruesome moments of Jess. Found dead near the swamp, the victim's pale hand still clutched a crumpled VIP pass to the recent concert. The singer, Leona, was the main attraction.

Deep in thought, Winston absentmindedly thumbed the murder weapon, a well-crafted sai. The sai was brand new, still wearing the faint scent of the store – it was witty of Leona to buy it so recently... Leona's sai... that was found at the scene. With this new piece of information, he decided to pay the singer a visit during her late-night martial arts class.

Entering the practice room, Winston noticed Leona in the middle of an intense sparring session. Her instructor watched with clear admiration as she dodged blows, her expression intense and focused. She slid into stroke, parrying with a level of expertise that implied countless hours of training. The instructor had remarked on her swift improvement with the sa, speculating on the freshness of her acquisition.

After the session, catching her breath with graceful composure, Leona crossed the floor to speak with Winston. As they talked, a subtle shift towards true crime came over their conversation. The sparkle in Leona's eye contrasted against the seriousness of the subject matter. It was clear she was comfortable, almost enthusiastic, addressing crime scenarios, drawing similarities to real events in the documentaries she frequently watched and wrote about. 

As they walked through the venue, Winston observed Leona's possessions, pausing over what appeared to be a well-worn notebook filled with notes upon notes on various crime documentaries. Intriguingly, Winston remembered another reference to this notebook from an event-goer at a recent documentary screening he had attended. He had seen the same notebook in Leona’s hand as she bought her new sai and scribbled away fervently while the documentary ran. 

Winston remarked on the close proximity of the concert venue – only a stone’s throw away from the swamp. Leona explained the choice, explaining how she loved the allure of the swamp during night, something atmospheric and eerie about the location that added a unique edge to her concerts... 

"She headed towards the swamp... after the concert, going towards the place she loved." The innocent statement caught Winston by surprise. He had stumbled upon someone who had noticed Jess, after Leona's performance, walk blissfully towards the swamp, clutching her VIP pass – the scene of her untimely death.

As Detective Winston thanked Leona for her time, he looked back at the singer, her recently purchased sai cradled in her forearm skillfully as if it were an extension of her own body. Winston couldn't quite shake off the strange sensation that washed over him. Returning to the stillness of his own vehicle, not yet ready to move on, he just sat there under the starlight, trying to make sense of the eerie dance between the facts that were slowly crafting the narrative to this murder. The story had many more veiled layers waiting to be discovered — and some heavy curtains waiting to be lifted.

Winston found himself standing in Freya's living room, his eyes quickly falling on a display case filled with various medieval weapons including the peculiar missing spot of a sai. Freya positioned herself beside Winston, noting his interest in her unique collection, "Those ais hold a special place in my heart. A reminder of my martial arts training back in the day. Even last week, I was at the dojo practicing with my favorite, a sai."

"Interesting," Winston hummed, a non-committal sound as he mentally filed away the information. He peered at the open spot in the case shaping a sai- the exact style like the weapon found in Jess and seemingly missing from the collection. He remembered the local authorities report about a matching weapon disappearing recently. 

Shifting his focus back on Freya, Winston decided to delve deeper. "And you frequent the local dojo, am I correct?" 

"Yes," Freya piped, curious. "I was there just last week."

"And Jess," Winston moved on. "You seem to have spent quite a sum to gain some insight on her."

Flustered, Freya breathed heavily, "Yes, I hired a private investigator. Jess started playing games, bragging about dirt she claimed to have on me."

"How does bird-watching tie into these games?" Winston questioned, casually dropping a seemingly unrelated question.

Taken aback, Freya chuckled awkwardly, "Well detective, I do frequent the swamp near here to observe the local birdlife. And yes, my car was indeed spotted parked there recently."

Seizing the moment, Winston probed, "So you would be quite familiar with navigating the swamplands then?" 

Freya gritted her teeth, "Yes, Detective. As I said, I often go there. My father taught me how to navigate those swamps."

Next he opened his folder, producing the letter meant for the local paper, written by Jess. Winston watched as Freya's reactions shifted from surprise to anger, to a controlled calm. It spoke volumes more than her carefully composed words, "Jess threw accusations left and right, yes. I asked our mutual friends to intervene, to convince her against disclosing these…misconceptions. But, you see, I also heard something disturbing about her. A woman fitting my description was seen heading towards the swamps.” Freya finished, eyes shimmering with unexpected tears.

Winston took a moment to consider her words, nodding slowly, "You've been very helpful, Freya. Thank you." His mind still picking on the revelations, the omissions, the twitches, keeping him aware that the game's just begun.

In the tranquil vineyards, Terry's life was brutally snuffed out by a makeshift shiv, and now it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the truth from suspects Bella and Jose.

The vineyard was unusually crowded as Winston steadily emerged from his car. Workers swarmed around an old bulldozer — an earsplitting roar clearly disrupting their conversation.

Leading towards the shade of the makeshift structure, Jose — a construction worker at the scene, caught Winston's eye. His brow was furrowed in worry. Laments about his diminishing performance at work were ripe among his co-workers. Noticing a murder of crows flocking in the field, an eerie feeling washed over Winston.

Approaching the blue-collar worker, Winston kicked-off casually, "Got a minute, Jose?"

Drawing a deep breath, Jose turned around to shrug, he seemed a bit frazzled. His friendly banter with his co-workers cut short due to a bulldozer malfunctioning, "It's an early lunch... not like I was doing much today. My boss caught me chattin' instead of workin'."

Chuckling, Jose bobbed towards the group of his co-workers, who were noticeably enjoying their conversation. "We've been going at it round the clock to get that wine store ready. Work's been tough lately, my performance has taken a hit, we gotta vent, right?"

"Yes, of course," Winston agreed, casually adding, "Isn't Terry your boss?"

"Technically, yes," sighed Jose, rubbing his neck nervously. "He owns this whole place," gesturing around the vineyard. "We had a... disagreement this morning. He accused me of stealing from the building site, falsifying work hours. Even threatened to fire me."

As Jose's voice trailed off, Winston observed, "Sounds tough."

"Yes, sir," Jose replied quietly. "The man even suspects me for the murder that happened here last week, during my shift. If Terry fires me... everything comes crashing down. This is the main work I've got right now... I can't afford to lose it."

Winston nodded understandingly and asked him if Terry, who was also present during the murder event, was around the vineyard at this time, to which Jose confirmed.

After reassuring Jose, he'd look into the matter, Winston began walking towards his car. Just as he was leaving, the obnoxious screech of the faulty bulldozer marked the end of an early lunch break.

Winston sipped his black coffee as he stared out of his aging police cruiser, eyeing the sprawling vineyard and thinking about Terry. Reports had come in of a heated exchange between Terry and Bella. A scenario that happened right after Terry caught Bella red-handed with a bottle of rare, expensive wine she hadn't paid for. An intern. Bella, whose name had been brought up more and more frequently in recent times due to her increasing thieving activities. 

She hadn't left the vineyard that day. Bella, who was spotted near the shed just minutes before Terry's body was found there. It was adding up, and something heavy was pressing on Winston's gut. He quietly exited his cruiser and walked over to Bella, who was diligently maintaining the vineyard's tools after work. 

"Ma'am," Winston began. His greeting was met with a simple nod from Bella.

"Bella, correct?"

"Yes, Sir," she replied.

"You were here all day?"

She nodded. "Everyone around here can tell you that," she murmured. 

An old red-and-green painted shed stood in the distance. He knew Bella had the privilege of going in and out without supervision. A luxury that troubled him, especially given her recent knack for stealing. 

"Busy day today?" Winston asked, glancing at Bella's hands.

"Always. I keep these tools as clean and sharp as possible," she replied, holding up a newly sharpened pruner. Her delicate hands belied the hardened steel of the instruments. 

Winston nodded, casting his gaze to one of the metal figurines intricately sculpted by Bella herself. 

"You do this?" he asked, pointing. 

Bella nodded, a small smile flashing across her face. She seemed to relish the precision, the skill required, and the metalwork. It was clear she was good at this. His eyes narrowed slightly as he put the figurine back down.

Her penchant for stealing wasn't just limited to the tools or anything she could lay her hands on. It was whispered around the vineyard that Bella had a keen taste for the wine here. Especially the rare and pricey varieties, which had been disappearing more frequently than before. Terry wasn't a fan though, especially after catching her in the act. Winston had found himself unusually bothered by what was open knowledge. Particularly, Terry's threat to report Bella to management if it continued.

On his way back to his cruiser, Winston remembered a particularly vivid memory from his briefing; Terry shouting at Bella right in front of the shed. The memory sent a chill running down his spine. He wore a stoic face in front of her, nodded in acknowledgment, and walked away. His gut was telling him that she had more to say, and he planned to stick around. Somewhat of a sixth sense, he attributed it to his years on the force.

Detective Winston watched an overhead view drone recording of the last soccer game. There had been a commotion, then Ivy had dropped suddenly, spilling her drink. He noted Meredith, a familiar figure most Saturdays there. He took the time to reflect on the girl: she liked her soccer, tending to show up religiously for the weekend games. 

Ivy, from the small bits of information he had, was someone that would frequent Meredith's shop. "Meredith's," he pondered, "it was quite a hotspot among the locals."

With this information in hand, Winston decided to pay a visit to Meredith at her coffee shop. Stepping inside, the bustling noise and smell of fresh coffee overwhelmed him. Meredith took her job seriously and always wore religious symbols, taking the time to pray before her shifts.

As he stood at the counter waiting for his usual, a loud bout of laughter broke out from a table nearby. For a split second, Winston saw an identical upset expression on Meredith. It reminded him of the CCTV footage he’d watched of Ivy laughing mercilessly.

Winston broke the silence, "I see Ivy used to come here often. She had a standing order I believe?"

Meredith was already preparing Winston's coffee. She glanced up, "Yes, Ivy was a regular customer of mine. She always drank what I prepared for her without questioning it."

There was something that niggled at Winston as she said those words, but he brushed it off, deciding to dig into something that had been on his mind. "I've heard you mixed drinks for Ivy sometimes, at the games?"

Meredith was nonchalant, "Yeah, I've mixed drinks in the past. People never detect the taste."

Winston acknowledged it with a nod as Meredith wrapped up their transaction, moving onto her next customer.

Before he left, he had one last question, "How did you feel when you heard Ivy making fun of your religious beliefs?"

Something flashed in Meredith’s eyes, "Anyone who disrespects my religion deserves severe punishment. I believe it, Detective, even if it's not the popular opinion."

Winston nodded, dropping a tip in her jar. It was clear there were layers to the barista and the spacious coffee shop that hinted at her prolific work. An array of different substances she uses for her drinks smiled back at him from the shelves behind the counter.

As he exited, his mind was full of information; Ivy's last moments at the match, the turn up of both ladies every Saturday, the relentless jibe of Ivy at Meredith's beliefs, and the latter's fierce defense of her faith. He patted his pocket recording device reassuringly - the interview was just the beginning.

Looking at Ivy's lifeless body sprawled on the soccer field, Winston couldn't help but feel anger at the unforgiving world; but he had learned long ago that serving justice was his ultimate duty. Ivy was an enthusiastic attendee of local sports events, always with a drink in her hand to enjoy the game. 

Justice needed to be done, and his first suspect was Hugo. He had been working as the sound engineer for the soccer match. Hugo was seen leaving the match that day, his departure unnoticed in the hustle and bustle of the game, raising no alarms. 

Winston decided to explore Hugo's professional life further and visited the sound studio a few blocks away from the soccer field where Hugo worked. Hugo was known to work with chemicals daily while fine-tuning the sound mixing. A side gig for a sound engineer, Winston mused. 

However, a visit to Hugo's studio revealed something more interesting. Tucked away in a corner, he discovered Hugo's private office. Secluded, it offered an intimate setting where Hugo would often meet with people. Confidential files peeked through the piles on his cluttered desk, hinting at the private meetings happening in his office.

During a conversation with one of Hugo's coworkers, Winston learned something intriguing. "Yeah, Hugo's got a license for private investigation," he said, "dunno why a sound engineer would need it, but yeah, he does." 

A particularly chilling fact that was the talk of the office was how Hugo also served drinks during the match...a bit unusual, even for a sound engineer. Unusual indeed, Winston thought to himself. 

Delving deeper into Hugo's background, it was revealed that he had taken a toxicology course in the past, a detail that raised a red flag in Winston's mind.

Hugo had a private office, a place to meet people, a shady license for private investigation, and knowledge of toxicology. All loose ends... that juggled around in his mind as Winston paved his way to finding Ivy's killer. Nonetheless, it was the responsibility of the reader to connect the dots. Winston left Hugo's office, clutching onto facts that needed to be put together to solve the mystery.

Meredith often spoke publicly about being a staunch follower of her religion and openly declared – more times than Winston would care to count – that anyone who disrespects her beliefs deserves severe punishment.

Right when the morning rush started to wear off, Meredith slipped into the backroom, tugging off her apron. Winston’s eyes landed on a bag near the entrance - a familiar logo from the local butcher shop from where she regularly purchased raw meat.

In the midst of the bustling shop, Winston's attention was drawn to a framed photograph. Meredith was captured mid-spit, a chicken wing in hand.

"But she only buys raw meat," the butcher's words echoed in his mind, contrary to the image he was witnessing. He recalled Meredith’s friends' words: "Meredith has never had cooked meat in front of us."

With lunchtime approaching, the crowd began to ebb and Winston found a moment to delve deeper. In a passing query, he asked, "Heard about the news? Ivy, laughing at your beliefs - that was caught on camera."

Meredith’s hands clenched a coffee cup so tightly it overflowed. In her eyes burned recognition and some suppressed pain. She merely muttered how disrespectful Ivy was.

A customer chimed in, ordering a highly customized drink and Winston’s observation heightened as he watched Meredith expertly mask all traces of the various ingredients she used in the drink. A craft eerily similar to certain practices of subterfuge.

As Winston reached out to accept his coffee—an all-black with a splash of half and half, he pondered over the peculiar pieces of the jig-saw. His goodbye was met with a cautionary note from Meredith, "Hey detective, respect every belief you come across... seems like the world could use more of that, you know?”

As Winston stepped onto the sidewalk, Meredith’s words left him with a chilling twist in his investigation.

Sophia's living arrangements reflected her financial ruin. A note from Mackenzie, garishly displayed on her wall, hinted at the ultimatum over art funds unless Sophia cleaned up her act, a common maneuver in attempts at addiction intervention.

Meeting Bruce at the entrance to the rainforest the following day, Winston sized him up. Nothing about his demeanor suggested guilt. Despite fearing the legal consequences of his actions, there was a calm about Bruce. For someone raised in the rainforest, he seemed one with the environment, he was comfortable in it.

Winston asked Bruce about his usual activities in his favorite retreat, prompting him to say, "I usually just like to be alone here, sir. A few chops here and there with my hatchet helps maintain the paths and keeps me busy."

Bruce’s answer inclined Winston to inquire, “And where is this hatchet now?” 

With a frown, Bruce replied, “I couldn’t find it today, sir. I usually keep it well maintained and in its usual spot.”

Their talk was interrupted by a passerby, jogging down a path. After briefly chatting about the area and visitor trends they noticed, the jogger mentioned that they hadn't seen anyone else in the rainforest that particular day, let alone someone leaving. The jogger left. Bruce turned back to Winston and shared, "Nobody usually notices me here, even when leaving the rainforest. It’s quite secluded.”

The thought of Peyton's gruesome death by the hatchet wound came back to Winston's mind. He abruptly thanked Bruce for his time and walked away.

The rainforest echoed with the weighted silence of the untold, and, as Winston ventured back to the city, a haunting thought lingered. The quiet, confident Bruce, with his missing hatchet, was confirmed to have been alone the last day Peyton was seen alive, and as the jogger had informed, unseen when he left the rainforest; the same day Peyton died.

Winston examined the manifest from Norris's ferry one final time. It matched up with what he already knew: Peyton had indeed been aboard Norris's ferry on the day he was killed. Winston took one last look at the document before folding it and tucking it away into his coat pocket.

Norris, the ferry captain, had a reputation amongst the barflies at his favorite local watering hole. They'd often overheard him detailing possibly too realistic scenes from the books they discussed at his thriller murder novel themed book club. Norris would get into specifics that made the members uncomfortable, his eyes often taking on an excited shine while he spoke of these gruesome and too-detailed-to-be-fiction murder scenes.

Tapping his notepad with a worn-down pen, Winston glanced up as Norris approached. Clad in his usual captain's garb and appearing a bit rough around the edges from years of running the ferry. Norris acted as the key traveling back and forth to the local rainforest, the last known place Peyton was seen alive.

"Captain Norris?" Winston asked, even though he already knew the answer. Norris nodded in confirmation, his steady gaze meeting Winston's. "Been doing this job for years," Norris said, a hint of pride reflected in his voice.

"It's a sturdy vessel you have," Winston commented as he gestured towards the ferry, his eyes landing on a standalone toolbox propped up near the bow. One item in particular stood out from the rest— a hatchet, well-used and worn, clear evidence of its frequent use in the maintenance of the ship under Norris's experienced hands.

"Ah, yes. That's Gertrude," Norris responded, referencing the hatchet, drawing Winston's attention back to him. Considering he was the only ferry giving rides to that rainforest, it was crucial Norris kept the ferry in good shape.

Winston then redirected the conversation, "We have a record of a Peyton. Took your ferry to the rainforest on the day of the murder. Anything you recall?"

Norris took a moment to recall, his brow furrowing in concentration. "Hmm... Peyton? Yeah, sure. He was one of my passengers that day."

After a few more hours of questioning, Winston returned to his squad car. The rainforest still lay heavy in his mind, and Peyton was a name he would not forget. But for now, he had everything he could glean from Norris, the ferry captain. His path forward would have to reveal itself in time.

Winston sat at the rustic wooden table of the steakhouse he frequented, waiting for his weekly interviewee to arrive. He liked to familiarise himself with the locals and their routines, it often helped him with his cases.

A few moments later, in came Bruce. Winston knew him to spend most of his time in the rainforest, mostly alone. In fact, he was out there alone on the time of the dreadful incident. Peyton, Bruce's father, was found in the rainforest with a hatchet wound.

"Bruce," Winston greeted him as he approached their table. The young man nodded in reply. He seemed distracted, perhaps the pressure of the situation was affecting him.

Bruce ordered his usual - a steak 'blue'. The regular chef confirmed his order. It wasn't unusual, Bruce preferred his meats raw. Recently at a family barbecue, he was panned a juicy cooked burger but he asked them to peel a fresh, raw version instead. He stated that it tasted more natural, primal to have it uncooked.

In their conversation, Winston learned about Bruce's handyman skills, and his special affection towards his hatchet. He used his hatchet to do most of his chores in the rainforest, and it was maintained admirably. Unfortunately, it was reported to be missing on the day his father was found dead.

Winston waited for Bruce to finish his meal before they ventured out towards the rainforest. Twilight was settling in, and the sounds of the night were emerging.

"Did anyone see you leave the forest that day?" Winston asked, as they ambled along the rainforest trail.

"No, nobody did. I was alone," Bruce replied, his voice barely audible amongst the chorus of rainforest creatures.

Winston nodded, asking no more questions as they walked along the darken path.

Winston put down the photos of the murder scene and decided it was time to converse with Norris. He had to travel to the ferry docks for this. The rainforest, where Peyton was found, was still drenched from the heavy rains just as Winston pulled into the wharf. 

Looking at the lineup of ferries floating lazily against the dock, he saw that only one sign pointed towards the rainforest - “Norris’s Ferry”. 

“Hello, detective,” Norris hailed Winston from the deck, setting down a heavily used hatchet and a wooden board he was working on. 

“Norris, is it? You’ve been a ferry captain for quite some time now?”

“Aye, sir. Many years. Through sun, rain and storm, the waters are like my backyard,” Norris replied.

“And Peyton. I understand he crossed these waters with you just recently?”

“Yeah. On the day of...the incident,” Norris replied, looking inconsolable as he confirmed Winston's words, “We had a bit of an argument.”

“Argument, you say?”

Norris heaved a sigh and grabbed a toolbox near his feet. He opened it revealing a various assortment of tools including the hatchet. Norris took a moment before confessing, “Peyton accused me of a past I’d rather forget. Told everyone on the ferry about my old fraud cases. A harsh reminder of a time I’d long left behind.”

A profound silence fell between them as the seas gurgled rhythmically against the ferry. It looked like Peyton's accusations had stung Norris. 

Winston pressed further. “What kind of rumors was Peyton spreading about you?”

Norris glanced away, looking out towards the sea. “Said I wasn’t the man people here thought I was. He tarnished my reputation. Made me a laughing stock.”

“The last time anyone saw Peyton was on your ferry. Do you recall anything unusual?”

“There was that argument, and he seemed distraught. Said he wanted to step away for a bit and enjoy the rainforest. I didn't see him again.”

“And you’re the only ferryman to the rainforest?”

“Yes, detective. However, once we dock, folks usually take their own paths. I don't keep track of them. Peyton was one of them.”

“Well, thank you for your time, Norris.” Winston handed him his card. “I will be in touch if I need anything further.”

As Winston walked away, he took a last glance at the ferry. Norris had resumed his work. Once again the sound of the hatchet echoed off the water, a solemn reminder of the grim nature of his visit.

“Hello, Ivy,” he said, his gaze piercing through her.

Dropping her head down, the terror and desperation in Ivy’s eyes were evident. Caught in a blackmail situation over deep secrets that Vanessa had threatened to reveal, secrets that could ruin her reputation, it was serving harsh punishments on her livelihood in the form of lost customers. She feared her secrets would come out any day now. It was this fear that had greeted Winston when Ivy arrived at the synagogue that morning, noticeably before Vanessa's life was tragically ended there.

"Wonderful sermons," Winston went on, "I heard about the incident at the synagogue, terrible loss for us all. Vanessa was such a wonderful woman."

A tightening grip around her own worn hands was the only sign from Ivy that she felt the weight and severity of the situation, she offered a low, mournful "Yes," in agreement.

Leaving the scene, Winston drove the short distance to the local dojo owned and run by a man by the name of Clayton. Clayton was an ex-husband to the recent bride of Leroy, and an avid martial arts instructor. On driving to the dojo, nostalgic flashes of visits to the local bar sprung forth in Winston's mind. Memories of how locals had on multiple occasions, narrated tales of Clayton exploring the swamp alone and of how he also ran survival tours there. On the day of the murder, many people at the local bar saw Clayton getting into his car alone, painting a picture of his solitary routine.

Upon arriving, he found Clayton, kneeling before an illustrious collection of martial arts weaponry, that included a sai, the same weapon used in the murder of Leroy.  

"So, you collect these?" Winston asked, nodding at the weapons.

"It's part of the job," Clayton responded as he carefully set down the sai, "having a wide knowledge of martial arts weaponry. But yes, I have developed a personal collection." 

Winston ventured further, "I heard you run survival tours in the swamp."

Clayton chuckled. "Oh yes. I love exploring the swamp. It's like it's a part of me. Each corner, each nook, I know all of them like the back of my hand.”

Winston then mentioned Clayton's recent loss. "Your ex got married to Leroy shortly after your divorce... Must've been a real punch in the gut," he said, gauging Clayton’s reaction. 

Clayton grimaced then muttered, "Well, yeah, of course. Can't deny it stung a bit."  
"But you'd want her back--"

Without waiting for Winston to finish, Clayton interjected. "Yes, I would. But she made it clear she doesn't want a reconciliation as long as Leroy is around." 

As Winston left the dojo, he began to storyboard the potential narrative. A man still in love with his ex-wife who wed another man right after their divorce, seen alone on the day of her new husband’s murder, with a confession that the ex-wife did not want to reconcile as long as Leroy was alive. He had a lot to ponder.

Detective Winston strode into the lobby of the martial arts gym, taking in the sights of many people practicing their moves, some more graceful than others. His attention quickly moved to a woman near the back of the room, demonstrating a jarring, yet elegant, technique to her student with a sai. Recognizing her from a picture at his precinct, Winston confirmed it was Madelyn.

He recalled Leroy’s fitness schedule, and his plans to switch personal trainers, leaving Madelyn for her biggest competitor. Friends had mentioned conversations Leroy had with Madelyn's rival. Winston also knew from his sources, she had been in the vicinity when Leroy was on the phone discussing the change.

Madelyn had a reputation of changing her hair practically every week. She seemed to enjoy the variety and surprise. A confirmed fact when Winston had visited her residential premises discovering several multi-colored wigs.

Not wasting any time, Winston approached Madelyn after her demonstration. Madelyn agreed to go to the local coffee shop for a friendly chat. After a sputtered start, Winston was able to get Madelyn talking about her martial arts training, including the sai technique she used in her demonstration. A technique he knew was the cause of Leroy’s death.

Her unique weapon choice hadn't really surprised him. Given the dimension of martial arts Madelyn specialized in, he suspected the sai came from her collection. A trip to the local martial arts store had led him to a store owner who confirmed her recent purchase of a pair. As well, the owner remembered seeing Madelyn practicing with her new acquisition at a local gym.

Eventually, Winston brought up the subject of passports. He'd found an interesting assortment of passports in various names inside a filing cabinet at Madelyn's house. He recalled her flustered behavior earlier at the post office where she'd been spotted getting passport photos taken. She struggled to explain, her face blanching at what he might uncover.

The conversation ended on a note of betrayal, with Madelyn softly admitting her inner circle betrayals. Winston gathered the facts in his mind, of hair wigs, martial arts and betrayal. Whisking the rest of his untouched coffee, he left Madelyn at the table, lost in her own world of memories.

Yet Winston had a murder inquiry to solve and no amount of color-changing wigs or phony passports could disguise that fact. He walked away with a nod, thinking of the next steps he would take before approaching Madelyn again. Irrespective of what she chose to conceal, he believed in the truth unveiling itself, the truth of a victim named Leroy.

"Now that's an intriguing line of work, Glenn," Winston remarked. Glenn gave a shrug and an almost shy nod before further adding, "I like to keep curious, Detective. I find toxicology talks within dental science forums quite engaging." 

Winston made polite conversation, shifting discussion towards Ricky. "I take it he was in your care recently?"

With a hint of sadness, Glenn responded, "Yes, he only left here yesterday. He had some work required before the holidays."

Before leaving, Winston inquired about Glenn's morning activities, "I hear you're an avid bird watcher, Glenn?"

Laughing, Glenn replied, "Yes, Detective! Nothing like the soft chirping of birds at the break of dawn. I have been birdwatching by, funny enough, the swamp, this very morning."

The detective then revealed a rather puzzling piece of information, he had uncovered during his investigation. "Ricky was found dead in the very swamp, you were birdwatching today, killed by bleach," he stated matter-of-factly.

Glenn looked genuinely shell-shocked; fear slowly seeping into his gaze. Sensing his discomfort, Winston decided to leave him with one last piece of information, "One more thing, Glenn. Ricky had you listed as the beneficiary on his life insurance policy." Winston held out the document from his satchel, showing Glenn the listed beneficent's name was indeed his.

"And just last week you mentioned the high monetary benefits that such a policy could bring in, didn't you, Glenn?" Winston added, watching the shock travel from Glenn's face to his very feet.

Not waiting for an answer, Winston turned and left the dental clinic, leaving Glenn to his thoughts.

Winston wrinkled his nose at the pungent odour of the swamp. Someone had found Ricky's body among the overgrown weeds and murky waters. An unfortunate end he mused, standing within walking distance of the local prison nearby. As he prepared to interview a potentially connected party — Tessa, a chemistry teacher turned inmate, he ran over the facts in his mind. 

Her current occupation as a cleaner in the prison's system gave her access to various supplies, cleaning supplies in particular. There were rumours of her unauthorized experiments involving bleach which had spiralled her into trouble once. Moreover, she worked on a farm near this very swamp.

Walking through the steel encased hallways of the prison, Winston arrived at Tessa's workspace. Finding her face damp with sweat, the persistent clang of her efforts to clean reverberated in the small and dank concrete space. She paused when he called her, "Tessa," Winston began, his tone crisp and official. "I'm detective Winston. I understand you taught chemistry before your unfortunate incarceration." 

"Yeah, I did. Is my knowledge of chemistry a crime now too?" Tessa paused,-looking at him expectantly. 

"Investigating a crime scene, Ricky's body was found in a nearby swamp," Winston continued ignoring her comments. "Awfully close to the prison farm you've been working on."

She made no visible reaction to the news. Then crossed her arms, furrowing her brows. "What's that got to do with any of this? And why should I know him? There are hundreds of prisoners passing through these cells..."

Ignoring her defensive stance, Winston targeted a more interesting topic, "Word has it you've been passionately sharing some rather unique dreams with your cell mates?" 

Tessa stared at Winston blankly, and then nodded. "Yeah, dreams... dreams of dying. Dreams of new beginnings. Awfully real. I don't know why, but I felt compelled to share them, almost eagerly. Figured I needed some context to these vivid dreams, so I started visiting the prison library often."

"In the sections about spiritualism, death rituals, and reincarnation, I believe? Parts of the sections involving death and the afterlife?" Winston queried.

"Yeah, that's right. It soothes me, somehow," Tessa shrugged, resuming her duties.

Leaving her to her cleaning, he walked away, the vestiges of the swamp carrying a far more sinister weight now.

When Letti's lifeless body is found horrifically mutilated by a machete at a secluded mountain cabin, gritty Detective Winston faces a chilling whodunit featuring suspects Delilah and Eddie.

Gazing out at the tranquil scenery of the mountain cabin where Letti met her end, detective Winston pondered the information before him. He had another interview to conduct, and as the mountain breeze tousled his rigid hair, he couldn't help but be reminded of this case's unnerving details.

Eddie was an interesting character, to say the least. A musician of sorts, he was known for incorporating tricks using a machete into his performances. A peculiar stage craft that Winston couldn't begin to comprehend. Performing such stunts would require him to practice, possibly during his free time he spent camping on the outskirts of the city, with his trusted machete always by his side.

The mountain cabin reverberated with somber silence as Winston approached Eddie. He had been staying at the same cabin, having been invited by Letti for a song recording. It was reported that during his stay that Eddie had no other engagements to attend to; an oddity given that this time of year was bustling with music festivals.

"How's the stay been, Eddie?" Winston began, trying to ease Eddie into the conversation.

"Quiet," Eddie responded, his gaze drifting off into the vast span of the desolate mountainscape. "Just how I like it, you know. Helps with the creativity." 

There was an aromatic air to Eddie, of someone who had worked tirelessly to uphold their image in the light of public scrutiny. It was well-known that Eddie was sensitive about his image, keen to maintain the rising trajectory of his music career, a career he held close to his heart.

The cabin’s solitude was a stark reminder of what was at stake for Eddie. Letti, the soulful songbird she was, had managed to unravel a hidden part of Eddie's life that threatened to shatter the glass tower he had been building over the years: his secret drug addiction. Unfortunately, the discovery gave Letti the leverage to manipulate Eddie's successful music career.

Winston kept an attentive poker face while internally connecting the pieces of information.

"The thing is, Eddie," Winston began, his tone sober, "Letti wouldn't have invited you over for any ordinary recording."

"I know," Eddie sighed heavily before he added, "She held my career in her hands, detective."

His confession resounded through the empty cabin, the once picturesque view from the window shading into a grim canvas of their situation. With no one around for miles, Winston wondered what influence this isolation could have on the psyche of the person who was here.

"I reckon we meet again, detective," Eddie said, his voice just above a whisper, as Winston left the cabin.

Detective Winston pulled his car up to the secluded cabin. His visit was to Delilah, the godmother of the recently slain Letti. So far, the only evidence he had found was a machete, smeared with blood.

He knocked on the heavy oak door of her abode and Delilah greeted him with a passive stare. Before he could utter a word, she gestured him inside and they both sat down to chat. Delilah, interestingly, made it a point to hang her machete over the fireplace, “Papa taught me to handle a machete since I was teen. I live out here alone in the wilderness, y'know, just as precaution.” she justified.

Their conversation flowed smoothly until Winston asked Delilah about her past. Instantly, the woman fell silent, her gaze fixed on a spot on the wall, as if she was lost in thought. She curtly responded, "I had a normal, happy childhood. That's all." Winston was struck by this as he knew from others' accounts that no one had ever heard her talk about her childhood or school days in detail.

Winston decided not to probe further, giving Delilah space to guide the conversation. This led her to casually mention her skills with a machete. Come to think of it, she’d won several local machete handling competitions. "I practice regularly," she added, a briefly proud glint in her eyes.

Winston nodded in acknowledgment, his mind returning to documents found in Letti’s possession. These documents seemed to implicate Delilah in some illegal activities. Letti reiteratively voiced concern about her godmother's activities. In fact, she had directly confronted Delilah about the evidence she’d stumbled upon. Even more alarmingly, Letti had confided in her friends about her intention to go public with this evidence.

Letti’s friends shared with Winston how she was deeply worried about Delilah's suspicious activities; however, the specific details of her past remained obscured. Winston took a last glance at the machete hanging over the fireplace before leaving the cabin, a sense of unsettling curiosity lingering in his mind.

In her living space, an enormous filing cabinet stood imposingly, filled to the brim with newspaper clippings. Winston could tell she was fond of keeping up with recent events. Also, the sheer size of the cabinet suggested it might be Gloria’s version of a living room.

Murray, the victim, had frequently been in the office late at night. Alone. Even secretive at times. Winston remembered spotting Murray meeting behind the stage with members of a rival dance group. Something didn't feel right and he paid more attention.

Winston recollected a heated quarrel between Gloria and Murray. Gloria was upset that Murray had leaked her proprietary choreography to the rival dance troupe. This discovery was devastating for Gloria. Her unique, innovative work was out in the open, her career was taking a steep plunge.

Winston stood up and glanced around once more before moving toward the office stairs. Notably, the rehearsal space had no security cameras - no direct way to monitor or record any unusual activities.

He found Gloria still hard at work in the office. She looked up and he could see disappointment and frustration etched on her lined face. "Work hard, but don't work yourself into the ground," Winston commented mildly. 

Gloria smiled ruefully, fingers splayed across scattered scripts and documents, "In this line of work, detective, there isn't much of a choice". 

He only nodded in response but inside, Winston felt a swirl of questions rising up. Unseen connections forming and dissipating too quickly to catch. Time to dig a little deeper.

Winston carried a cup of his favorite diner's coffee in his hand as he walked into Murray's office building. A player had accidentally ingested cleaning fluid during a practice session and had fallen ill. The report confirmed that Chris was the coach at the time of the incident.

Winston nodded, thinking of Chris's coaching duties operating during the same hours. In the hallowed silence of a synagogue, a shocking murder unfolds as Derek is impaled by a harpoon, leaving Detective Winston with two unlikely suspects – Hailey and Angela.

Winston idly flicked his cigarette ash onto the pavement as he studied the crime scene photos spread out on the hood of his car. His stone-set face showed no emotions as he shuffled through the pictures of Derek ladled onto the cold marble splashed with ink and blood.

His eyes narrowed slightly as he picked up a photo of what could only be a harpoon. Blinking slowly in contemplation, Winston accepted this as a clue, however strange, and pocketed the photo.

He pulled out another, a picture of a gang tattoo, and subsequently made his way towards his next suspect.

Arriving at the edge of the harbor, he could smell the salty breeze that carried a strong odor of fish and seaweed. Loosely tethered to the slippery wooden dock with expertly tied knots, the sign of someone familiar with ropes, the fishing vessel stood tall and forbidding, bristling with equipment that included several harpoons. He saw the figure of a woman hauling baskets of fresh catch onto the quayside. Her muscles flexed under the strain, but she moved easily and without breaking a sweat.

"Hailey?" Winston questioned, the name hanging heavy in the air between them.

"That's me," she replied, shooting him a glance, but continuing with her task.

"I see your job keeps you in shape," Winston stated, noting her above-average strength with a subconscious nod.

In response, Hailey shrugged, "It pays, and the work isn't half bad."

Hailey radiated an aura of authority. This was her world, she belonged here and the others respected her. One of her coworkers passed by, tipping his head in acknowledgement towards Hailey, "Evening, sister," he greeted. 

Winston noticed the respect she commanded. He also noticed the way her colleagues avoided looking at her—or rather, the tattoo inked to her arm. 

Before Winston could enquire further, a family passed by them. A group of kids laughing and shoving at each other, a remote jammed into the hands of Hailey as they settled onto a nearby couch.

"Movie night?" Winston asked and received an affirmative nod from her. "Yeah and nobody likes the movies I pick but it's my house so it's my rules."

Intrigued, Winston glanced at the television. His eyebrows raised slightly as he noted the opening scene of a classic crime thriller.

"They don’t usually complain when they don't have the remote though, do they?" he asked, pointing towards the small device.

Hailey smirked, a recognition sparking in her eyes, "Nah. They know better than that."

Amidst all this, Winston noticed a book beneath the coffee table as he turned to leave. Taking a closer look before departing the apartment, he realized it was "The Psychology of Criminal Minds", a book known for its study on famous serial killers. 

Noticing his focus on the book, Hailey nonchalantly yawned, indicating a late-night reading habit and added, "Gets me through the night when I can't sleep. Weird preference for late-night read?" She shrugged as if it were nothing, the faintest spark of defiance reflecting in her steely eyes.

Before Winston could get a word in, a fellow gang member approached Hailey, muttering something about Derek’s latest public speech disrespecting their gang. Her face stiffened. 

"We'll deal with it," Hailey said, her voice tightening, her demeanor shifting. She glanced briefly at Winston, quickly reading his inquisitive expression, and added, "It's not good to let people trash talk your family."

With that, she sent Winston on his way, staying behind to discuss amongst her 'family' the disrespect Derek had shown towards them.

As Winston loaded up into his car, his thoughts traveled to her book and her expertise with rope ties. The knots were made by someone who knew their way around a rope, and her job on the fishing vessel could’ve easily taught her that.

With that, Winston drove off into the evening, the crime scene photos shuffling on the passenger seat.

Winston found himself entering the grand synagogue. A revered place of worship that gathered a tight-knit community. The murder of Derek had sent shockwaves through the community, threatening to disrupt the tranquility of the sacred space.

Standing under the magnificent dome, Winston noticed Angela, Derek's grandmother who was a highly respected member of the community. She was absorbed in polishing a large silver key - clearly bestowed only to trusted insiders of the community. She appeared not to notice Winston's arrival.

As Winston made his presence known, Angela seemed startled but quickly masked her emotions. 

"My apologies for the intrusion, Ma’am. I am here about Derek," Winston delicately approached the subject.

Even though her face remained neutral, the flinch in her eyes revealed her disturbance. "That's quite alright, detective..." she started, her grip tight around the key.

Winston caught sight of her unusually strong hands and robust arms – strange for an elderly woman in her society. Upon asking, he discovered Angela has been an avid fisherwoman since she was a child and had won many titles at local fishing competitions. Her robustness was plausibly from her fishing background.

Despite her attempt to evade pressing questions, Angela seemed uncomfortable and hastily brought the conversation to her past and future challenges in the fishing competitions with Derek. Her anxiety seemed tied to the challenges Derek brought forward and the atmosphere would tense every time Derek's challenge escalated. Derek really got to Angela, making her feel threatened and pushed at her limits in these competitions.

"I remember Derek grinning over that photo; where he caught you secretly betting against him in the last competition," Winston probed. "He told me he intended to expose you at the upcoming one."

Angela's reaction suggested his words hit a nerve, "You see, Detective... Derek, he...knew something. He found proof of my betrayal. He confronted me about it, claimed he would tell everyone if I didn't stop it. I would lose everything."

Winston registered the shock in his eyes. She had unwittingly given him the most crucial lead. Was this betrayal solely related to the fishing competitions or was there something even more sinister?

As Winston prepared to leave, Angela asked, "Do you think this could have escalated beyond our fishing rivalry? Derek confronting me about the bets and all..."

He chose not to comment, giving Angela an assuring smile before leaving. But the words lingered in his mind long after he left the synagogue. The certainty was that Angela's secret was at risk of exposure. Derek knew, confronted her, had proof, and threatened to share it. Angela felt cornered and threatened - enough to resort to desperate measures?

As he stared pensively at the large synagogue receding in his rear-view mirror, Winston pieced together the web of events and motives pointing at Angela. Derek's death in the synagogue, Angela's robust fishing skills, her betrayal, Derek’s confrontations, the high-stakes competition, the key, and her fear—it seemed like the seemingly kind grandmother Angela was not as innocent as he initially thought.

In the middle of pliés and pirouettes, a deadly crossbow bolt finds its mark, leaving Ryan lifeless in the dance studio and launching Detective Winston into a tense pas de deux with suspects Rex and Mandy.

Detective Winston had barely finished his coffee when he received the call about the murder at the dance studio. Ryan, a notable figure and beloved dance instructor and advocate for racial integration, was found dead in the wee hours of the morning. The news from the officer stated that there was only one person present, Rex, at the time of the murder. 

Crossbow, a peculiar choice of weapon, but Rex was a known historical weapons enthusiast and was found alone in the studio. Rex was a man known in the community to frequently utter his disgust and hatred for other races. He never shied away from making his views known and didn't even care about the public backlash he received.
